case_study_insert.main_stem: Fenwick Precision Moulds (FPM) is a private limited company in the industrial tooling sector in the West Midlands, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Rowan Fenwick, it designs and machines injection moulds and dies for automotive and appliance makers and uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. FPM plans to invest $640,000 in a 3D printing and CAM tooling cell, financed by $380,000 retained profit and $260,000 under hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $196,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. FPM faces rising labour turnover and a defect rate of 3.8% on moulded tool components.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The tooling shop completed 8,400 mould and die components last quarter at a defect rate of 3.8%, up from 2.4% a year earlier. Customer complaints about delivery rose from 11 to 26 per month. Average lead time extended to 14 days from 9 days. Market research of 260 appliance and automotive buyers found that 53% would pay up to $0.70 more for faster tooling, and 42% rank precision finish highest. A skills audit shows 12 of 40 staff need CAM programming training; on-the-job coaching is offered, off-the-job college courses cost $820 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.30 to $14.07 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills. (3) Tool steel and polymer resin input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while automotive tooling orders grew 2.9%.

questions.question_text: FPM plans to finance part of its $640,000 tooling cell with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for FPM of using the $380,000 retained profit instead of hire purchase.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or lease charges, so FPM avoids the financing cost attached to the $260,000 hire-purchase agreement on top of fixed costs of $196,000 a year. That protects cash flow while the 3D printing and CAM cell is installed and helps absorb the 5.8% wage rise and the 10.6% rise in tool steel and resin costs without increasing the $16.00 price. Uncommitted cash also covers the 12 staff needing CAM training.

Point 2: Using retained profit means ownership of the tooling cell passes to FPM immediately, with no hire-purchase lender holding title until the final instalment. Rowan Fenwick and the shareholders keep full control of how the equipment is used, and there is no repossession risk if automotive tooling orders soften, so the $380,000 can be combined flexibly with the hire-purchase funding rather than tied to fixed rental payments. That matters with a 3.8% defect rate and 26 complaints a month already pressing on resources.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to FPM and its $640,000 financing decision.

questions.question_text: FPM is promoting its faster precision tooling. Consider advertising in trade journals, exhibiting at an engineering trade fair, or using social media aimed at product designers. Which should FPM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Advertising in trade journals: Adverts in tooling magazines would reach appliance and automotive engineers and lend authority to the faster-tooling claim. The weaknesses are cost and weak targeting: many readers will not commission moulds, and a 40-employee firm with $196,000 fixed costs and a $640,000 cell cannot waste much spend, nor can it measure the enquiries generated.

Engineering trade fair: A stand allows buyers to handle sample moulds and discuss finish quality and the 3.8% defect rate with FPM's designers. It matches the 42% of surveyed buyers who rank precision finish highest, since the product can be inspected. The drawbacks are the stand cost, a short event window and the need to chase leads among the 260 buyers in the research sample quickly.

Social media aimed at product designers: Targeted posts can reach the 53% of buyers who would pay $0.70 more for faster tooling at low cost, with measurable clicks and fast feedback. It suits a small team and supports the new CAM cell, but designers often need to see a physical tool before placing an order, so social media alone may create interest without conversions.

Recommendation: FPM should choose the engineering trade fair as the primary launch route, backed by low-cost social media follow-up. Handling the moulds directly overcomes finishing concerns for the 42% who rank precision highest and reaches specifiers efficiently. Trade journals are rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a small company; social media alone is rejected because physical inspection matters for tooling, so it should support rather than replace the fair.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to FPM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of FPM with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of FPM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade journals and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: FPM's defect rate is 3.8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for FPM of replacing laissez-faire leadership with a more democratic style among its 40 staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would involve the 40 staff in decisions about the new CAM tooling cell, raising job satisfaction and addressing the rising labour turnover. Machinists who help set tool-setting routines are likelier to take care over finish, directly reducing the 3.8% defect rate and the complaints that rose from 11 to 26 a month in FPM's flat structure. Maslow's higher-order needs are met by being consulted, so motivation improves without relying only on pay.

Point 2: Regular consultation surfaces practical improvements from the people running the machines, cutting rework without extra capital beyond the $640,000 cell. Herzberg would see the added responsibility as a motivator, so staff take pride in precision finish, the factor 42% of buyers rank highest. Higher involvement builds commitment, reducing the cost of replacing skilled staff and the $820 per employee training expense, and protecting output of 50,000 components while the 3D printing and CAM cell beds in and the 14-day lead time is tackled.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FPM's defect rate, turnover, workforce and training costs.

questions.question_text: FPM must train 12 staff to operate the new CAM cell. Consider on-the-job coaching or off-the-job college courses at $820 per employee. Which should FPM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Coaching on FPM's own machines is specific to the CAM tooling cell and its finish standards, avoids the $820 per person fee for 12 staff, a saving of $9,840 (12 × $820), and keeps staff productive while learning. That protects the 8,400 components completed last quarter and helps reduce the 3.8% defect rate. The weaknesses are that coaches are taken off their own work, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which could matter when 42% of buyers rank precision finish highest.

Off-the-job college courses: At $820 each, 12 staff cost $9,840, modest beside the $640,000 investment and easy to arrange away from the shop floor. External courses bring up-to-date CAM programming and a recognised qualification, useful with rising labour turnover and support for the 53% who would pay $0.70 more for faster tooling. However, staff are away from the shop floor, reducing capacity on the new cell, and generic content may not match FPM's exact tooling settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: FPM should choose on-the-job coaching first, with short external modules for senior designers. Coaching is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids output loss while the defect rate is 3.8%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 12 of 40 staff off the floor and spending $9,840 would slow commissioning of the $640,000 cell and still require on-site reinforcement; certification can be added later once the cell is stable and the 14-day lead time is reduced. The $9,840 saved can instead support the cover of $196,000 fixed costs while the 14-day lead time is reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to FPM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of FPM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of FPM with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how FPM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $196,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $196,000 ÷ $7.00 = 28,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 28,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways FPM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 28,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 50,000 components gives a margin of safety of 22,000 units, showing headroom to fill the $640,000 CAM cell before losses begin.
2. Contribution of $7.00 a component lets FPM test the $0.70 premium for faster tooling; if the 53% of buyers accept it, contribution would rise to $7.70 and the $196,000 fixed costs would be covered sooner.
3. Fixed costs of $196,000 and $7.00 contribution show the extra volume needed to meet the $260,000 hire-purchase payments, so targets can be set for automotive and appliance customers.
4. Average total cost of $12.92 a component ($196,000 ÷ 50,000 = $3.92 plus $9.00) can be tracked against the 3.8% defect rate to judge whether the new cell is reducing rework and to monitor the $9.00 variable cost as tool steel and resin prices rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 28,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 50,000-unit output; faster-tooling premium modelling; hire-purchase volume for the $260,000 commitment; and average total cost of $12.92 to monitor defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate FPM's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has FPM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.55 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.11 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.04 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $44,000 inventories + $72,000 trade receivables + $28,000 cash = $144,000; 2025 current assets = $58,000 + $96,000 + $24,000 = $178,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $144,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.60 and 2025 = $178,000 ÷ $115,000 = 1.55. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($144,000 − $44,000) ÷ $90,000 = $100,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.11; 2025 = ($178,000 − $58,000) ÷ $115,000 = $120,000 ÷ $115,000 = 1.04.

Evaluation: Liquidity has worsened. The current ratio fell from 1.60 to 1.55 as current liabilities rose sharply from $90,000 to $115,000, faster than current assets, which grew from $144,000 to $178,000. The acid test fell further, from 1.11 to 1.04, meaning FPM is more reliant on inventory to meet short-term obligations. Cash dropped from $28,000 to $24,000 while trade receivables climbed from $72,000 to $96,000, so sales are being made on credit but cash is not arriving quickly. With $260,000 of hire-purchase commitments and fixed costs of $196,000, that cash position is a concern despite the $640,000 investment in new capacity.

Conclusion: FPM's financial position has not improved. Both the current ratio (1.60 to 1.55) and the acid test (1.11 to 1.04) declined, so short-term solvency is weaker. The 1.04 acid test is the stronger evidence of concern because it excludes the $58,000 of inventories, some of which may be slow-moving given the 3.8% defect rate. Management should tighten credit control on the $96,000 of receivables before committing further funds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for FPM of using 3D printing in its new CAM tooling cell.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: 3D printing lets FPM prototype moulds quickly, helping cut lead time from 14 days and appeal to the 53% of buyers who would pay $0.70 more for faster tooling. Faster prototypes can also reduce the 3.8% defect rate because designs can be tested before hard tooling is cut, protecting the $7.00 contribution on each $16.00 component. Better finish also supports the 42% who rank precision highest.

Disadvantage: The $640,000 investment adds to fixed costs already at $196,000 a year, and 3D printing materials and machine maintenance are expensive. With 12 staff needing CAM training and rising labour turnover, FPM may lack the skills to exploit the technology, so the cell could sit underused and the 3.8% defect rate may persist while cash of $24,000 remains tight. Sending 12 staff for training would also lengthen the 14-day lead time, weakening the 53% speed-focused segment. The 26 monthly complaints show that finish problems are already hurting customer relations.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to FPM's lead time, research data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in tool steel and polymer resin input costs will affect FPM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): FPM's $260,000 hire-purchase agreement is the relevant commitment. If its cost tracks the 0.75 percentage-point base-rate rise, the illustrative annual addition is 0.75% × $260,000 = $1,950 (0.0075 × $260,000), a figure built only from insert numbers and labelled as illustrative because the agreement's exact terms are not stated. It is small beside $196,000 fixed costs; the $380,000 retained profit is unaffected by rates.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.07 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 40 but not hours worked, individual pay or the number on the minimum, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented. What can be derived is labour productivity: 50,000 components ÷ 40 staff = 1,250 components per worker. If that holds, the rise is absorbable; if the 3.8% defect rate or turnover lowers output, unit labour cost rises and the $7.00 contribution per component shrinks. The effect is genuine but cannot be precisely quantified from the data.

Input cost inflation (10.6% on steel and resin): The insert does not split the $9.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $9.00 rose 10.6%, it adds 10.6% × $9.00 = $0.95 per component, and at 50,000 components a year that is $47,500 (50,000 × $0.95). Even a partial rise compounds across all output and cuts contribution below $7.00, although the $0.70 faster-tooling premium could recover some of it.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in tool steel and resin will have the greatest impact. Its $47,500 bound is far larger than the illustrative $1,950 interest effect, it applies to every one of the 50,000 components, and it directly erodes the $7.00 contribution that must cover $196,000 fixed costs and the $260,000 hire-purchase commitment. The interest effect is small and based on an illustrative calculation; the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly offset through productivity of 1,250 components per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to FPM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on FPM with shown calculations where data allow.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of FPM using only shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgment.
